entries.topicDescription: Special class types for modeling data and restricted hierarchies.

tips.title: data class — instant value objects
tips.content:
Data classes auto-generate equals(), hashCode(), toString(), copy(),
and destructuring functions from the properties in the primary constructor.

Perfect for models, DTOs, and state holders — any class whose identity
is defined by its data rather than a unique reference.

Only properties declared in the primary constructor take part in the
generated equals(), hashCode(), toString() and copy(); properties declared in
the class body are ignored, which is a common source of confusion.

Use 'copy()' to create modified copies without mutating the original.
This is the foundation of immutable state management in Kotlin.
tips.codeSnippet:
data class User(val name: String, val age: Int)

val alice = User("Alice", 30)
val aliceCopy = alice.copy(age = 31)

println(alice)         // User(name=Alice, age=30)
println(alice == aliceCopy)  // false — different age

// Destructuring
val (name, age) = alice
println("$name is $age")  // Alice is 30

tips.title: sealed class — restricted hierarchies
tips.content:
A sealed class restricts which classes can extend it.
All direct subclasses must be defined in the same package and module.

This makes 'when' expressions exhaustive — the compiler ensures
you handle every possible subtype. No 'else' branch needed.

Sealed classes are perfect for modeling states, events, and results.
They're like enums on steroids — each subclass can hold different data.

tips.title: sealed interface — flexible sealed hierarchies
tips.content:
Since Kotlin 1.5, you can use sealed interfaces in addition to sealed classes.
A class can implement multiple sealed interfaces but can only extend one class.

This allows more flexible hierarchies where a subtype can belong
to multiple sealed groups simultaneously.

Sealed interfaces are great for modeling capabilities or cross-cutting
categories that don't fit into a single inheritance tree.
tips.codeSnippet:
sealed interface Error
sealed interface UserError : Error
sealed interface NetworkError : Error

// Can implement multiple sealed interfaces
data class Timeout(val ms: Long) : NetworkError
data class NotFound(val id: String) : NetworkError, UserError
data class Unauthorized(val reason: String) : UserError

fun handleError(error: Error) = when (error) {
    is Timeout      -> retry()
    is NotFound     -> show404()
    is Unauthorized -> redirectToLogin()
}

tips.title: A data class must follow a few rules
tips.content:
A data class needs at least one parameter in its primary constructor, and every primary-constructor parameter must be marked val or var. It cannot be abstract, open, sealed or inner. It can, however, implement interfaces and extend other classes.

These rules exist because the generated equals, hashCode, toString, copy and componentN functions are built from the primary constructor's properties. Only those properties take part.

tips.title: copy() is shallow
tips.content:
copy() creates a new instance and copies each property reference as it is. If a property holds a mutable object such as a MutableList, the original and the copy share the same list, so changing it through one changes it in the other.

For real immutability, keep collections read-only and replace them when you change something, or copy the inner structure explicitly when you need independent state.
tips.codeSnippet:
data class Team(val name: String, val members: MutableList<String>)

val a = Team("core", mutableListOf("Ana"))
val b = a.copy(name = "core-2")

b.members.add("Bo")
println(a.members)   // [Ana, Bo]  — the same list is shared!

// Safer: read-only list, replaced on change
data class Team2(val name: String, val members: List<String>)
val c = Team2("core", listOf("Ana")).let { it.copy(members = it.members + "Bo") }

tips.title: Use data object for singleton cases in a sealed hierarchy
tips.content:
A plain object has a default toString like Loading@1a2b3c and identity-based equality only. Declaring it as data object (stable since Kotlin 1.9) gives it a readable toString ("Loading"), and equals/hashCode that stay consistent even if a second instance is ever created (for example through reflection or deserialization), which makes it the right choice for the stateless cases of a sealed type.

Use a data class for cases that carry data and a data object for cases that don't.

tips.title: An else branch defeats exhaustiveness checking on sealed types
tips.content:
The main benefit of a sealed type is that a when over it must cover every subtype, so adding a new subtype turns every incomplete when into a compile error. If you add else -> ... to that when, the compiler is satisfied by the else and no longer tells you about new cases: they silently fall into the fallback.

Leave out else when you mean "handle every case", and spell out the cases you handle the same way. Use else only when the fallback is genuinely correct for every future subtype.

tips.title: Model screen state as a sealed type, not as a bag of flags
tips.content:
A single data class with isLoading, error and data fields can represent impossible combinations, such as loading and failed at the same time, and every screen has to remember which combinations are valid. A sealed interface where each case carries only the data that makes sense removes the impossible states.

The UI then uses an exhaustive when to render each case, and adding a new state (for example Empty) produces compile errors wherever it isn't handled.

tips.title: Mutating a var in a data class can break hash-based collections
tips.content:
A data class's hashCode is computed from its primary-constructor properties. If one of them is a var and you change it after the object has been put in a HashSet or used as a HashMap key, its hash changes, but it is still stored in the bucket for the old hash. The collection then can't find it: contains returns false and remove fails, although the object is still there.

Prefer val properties in data classes that are used as keys or in sets, and use copy() to create a changed instance.
tips.codeSnippet:
data class Point(var x: Int, var y: Int)

val points = hashSetOf(Point(1, 2))
val p = points.first()

p.x = 99                       // hashCode changed after insertion
println(points.contains(p))    // usually false — lookup goes to a different bucket
println(points.size)           // 1      — but it is still in the set
